Apple has long been pushing to collect commissions on app sales even when they occur through third-party platforms. This hardline stance has put the company at odds with the judge in its protracted legal battle with Epic Games.

The company subsequently submitted a more moderate proposal offering reduced commission rates, but acknowledged in new regulatory filings that such sales might ultimately yield nothing...

Apple's App Commission Fight

Antitrust regulators around the world have taken issue with Apple's practices: developers have historically been able to sell iPhone apps and in-app content only through Apple's official App Store. This monopoly position has allowed the Cupertino company to set commission rates at its own discretion, leaving iPhone developers with no choice but to accept them.

The European Union is the first region globally to force Apple to permit third-party app stores, while US courts have ruled that Apple must allow developers to offer in-app purchases and subscriptions through external payment platforms.

In the US case, Apple charges a 27% commission on in-app content sold outside the App Store—even though the transaction doesn't actually go through the App Store—a move that drew sharp criticism from the presiding judge. After deducting roughly 3% in payment processing costs, the commission rate Apple collects is effectively the same regardless of whether developers sell through Apple's store or not.

The judge noted that this clearly amounted to an abuse of the spirit of the ruling; Apple countered that the court had not specified an acceptable commission rate for external sales.

Lower Commission Rates

Apple recently submitted a more moderate commission proposal for sales outside the App Store.

  • Standard apps would be charged 15%, compared with the current 30% in-app purchase ("IAP") commission they must pay;
  • Video Partner Program ("VPP"), News Partner Program ("NPP"), Mini App Partner Program ("MPP"), and subscription renewals would be charged 10%;
  • Apps under the Small Business Program would be charged 5%.

The company hopes the court will view these discounted rates as reasonable, sufficient to reflect the costs of providing developers with Xcode and other tools that help them build apps.

But acknowledging it might ultimately get nothing

However, while Apple is seeking permission to charge the lower commissions outlined above, it acknowledged in new regulatory filings that the court may ultimately bar the company from collecting any commission at all on transactions conducted through third-party app stores and other external platforms. The Financial Times reports:

Analysts noted that services revenue could decline for the first time as a result, weighing on the company's valuation.
